Eating Well on a Motorcycle Tour

Proper nutrition might not sound as thrilling as mountain passes and coastal roads, but it's the fuel that keeps you alert and enjoying the ride. A hungry, dehydrated rider is a dangerous rider. Here's how to eat well on tour without breaking the bank or spending all your time cooking.

The Three Strategies

Most touring meals fall into three categories:

  • Self-catering: Cheapest. Requires a stove and basic supplies. Best for campers.
  • Pub and café meals: Mid-cost. Convenient, social, and you get local food. The backbone of most touring meal plans.
  • Supermarket grazing: Budget-friendly and flexible. Meal deals, sandwiches, snacks. No cooking required.

Camp Cooking Essentials

If you're camping, a compact stove setup opens up cheap and satisfying meals:

  • Stove: A simple screw-on gas canister stove (MSR PocketRocket, Jetboil) weighs under 200g.
  • Pot: A single 750ml pot handles everything from coffee to pasta.
  • Fuel: One 230g gas canister lasts 5-7 days of basic cooking.
  • Utensils: Spork, small knife, lighter. That's all you need.

Quick Camp Recipes

  • Porridge with honey: Oats, boiling water, a squeeze of honey. Ready in 3 minutes, fills you until lunch.
  • Pasta with pesto and cheese: Quick-cook pasta, a jar of pesto, grated cheese. 10 minutes, immensely satisfying after a long ride.
  • Super noodles plus: Instant noodles upgraded with a tin of tuna or sweetcorn. Cheap, fast, decent fuel.
  • Couscous with whatever: Couscous rehydrates with just boiling water. Add tinned fish, olives, sun-dried tomatoes from a deli counter.
  • Fry-up: If you have a small frying pan, bacon and eggs from a village shop is a luxury camp breakfast.
Hydration matters more than food on a motorcycle. Dehydration causes fatigue, poor concentration, and headaches — all dangerous when riding. Drink at least 2 litres of water per day, more in warm weather. Carry a refillable bottle and fill it at every stop.

Pub Grub Guide

Village pubs are the touring rider's canteen. Most serve excellent, hearty food at reasonable prices:

  • Lunch mains: £10-15. Pies, fish and chips, ploughman's, burgers.
  • Evening mains: £12-18. Steaks, local specialities, Sunday roasts.
  • Always try the local speciality: haggis in Scotland, Cornish pasties in Cornwall, Welsh lamb in Wales, Cumberland sausage in the Lakes.
  • Pub hours vary — most serve lunch 12-2pm and dinner 6-9pm. In rural areas, the kitchen may close early.

On-the-Road Snacking

Keep energy topped up between meals:

  • Flapjacks and cereal bars (high energy, don't melt, survive in a tank bag)
  • Trail mix with nuts and dried fruit
  • Bananas (potassium helps prevent cramps)
  • Jelly babies (quick sugar hit — a time-honoured cyclist's trick that works for bikers too)

Supermarket Stops

Major supermarkets along touring routes are excellent for resupply. Meal deals (sandwich, snack, drink for £3-4) are the touring rider's best friend. Stock up when you pass through a town — you don't know when the next one will be.

Eating well on tour is about balance: cook when it's practical, eat out when it's enjoyable, and always keep snacks within reach. Your body and your riding will thank you.
keyTakeaways: Touring meals fall into three strategies: self-catering, pub and cafe meals, and supermarket grazing.
A screw-on gas stove (MSR PocketRocket, Jetboil) and one 750ml pot handle most camp cooking.
One 230g gas canister lasts around 5-7 days of basic cooking.
Hydration matters more than food; drink at least 2 litres of water a day, more in warm weather.
Supermarket meal deals at £3-4 are the touring rider's most flexible cheap lunch.

faq.q: What is the cheapest way to eat on a motorcycle tour?
faq.a: Self-catering with a compact stove is by far the cheapest. Porridge with honey, pasta with pesto and cheese, or couscous with tinned fish cost pennies per serving. Supplement with supermarket meal deals for lunch at £3-4. Cook breakfast and dinner at camp and treat yourself to a pub meal once or twice across the week.

faq.q: What camp cooking kit do I need?
faq.a: A simple screw-on gas canister stove such as an MSR PocketRocket or Jetboil weighs under 200g, a single 750ml pot handles everything from coffee to pasta, and a spork, small knife and lighter complete the set. One 230g gas canister lasts roughly five to seven days of basic cooking, so you rarely need to carry spares on a week's tour.

faq.q: How much water should I drink while touring?
faq.a: Aim for at least 2 litres per day, and more in warm weather. Dehydration causes fatigue, poor concentration and headaches, all of which are dangerous on a bike. Carry a refillable bottle and top it up at every stop rather than buying bottled water, since UK tap water is excellent and free.

faq.q: When do rural pubs serve food?
faq.a: Most village pubs serve lunch from around noon to 2pm and dinner from 6pm to 9pm. In rural areas the kitchen may close earlier, so do not assume you can eat mid-afternoon or late evening. Carry snacks such as flapjacks, trail mix and bananas to bridge the gaps, and try local specialities like haggis, Cornish pasties or Cumberland sausage.
